rv.q: This subversive comedy is now a posh panto, directed by Max Webster.
Every nook and cranny of this brightly lit (thanks for the gaudiness, Jon Clark) production is ornate.
I loved it because it honours Wilde’s wit but also his radicalism and his embrace of artifice.
With its dazzle, joy and original anarchic spirit of pantomime, this is the most stylish festive show in town.

This gorgeous, joyously out-there staging feels almost like payback.

Over nearly three hours, this gossamer creation gets stretched very thin indeed, especially at the denouement, which here feels interminable.

And while I don’t want to be a party-pooper, a slight sense of exhaustion set in watching his concertedly exuberant, subtext-declaring Earnest, which amply suits the gaiety of the panto season and has its moments but isn’t really one for the annals.
It’s an utter delight, the perfect Christmas choice.
Fun, fabulous and fiery, it's a hoot.
Webster’s sparkling version brings out all the cutting observations of an Irish outsider looking in on the absurdities of English society.
I certainly left in high spirits—an early Christmas treat.
This is a vibrant celebration of a playwright who has just as much to say to the 21st century as he did to his own.
Big, bold, and beautiful, its star cast is matched by every element of its high-quality production value to create one of the strongest shows National Theatre have put on this year.

cn.t: Critics praise Max Webster's flamboyantly camp, hot-pink production as joyous and exuberant, with most celebrating its bold foregrounding of Wilde's queer subtext, though a few find the over-the-top approach excessive.
